summary: AgriShift AI is a student-built prototype for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. This 30-second demo explores a hypothetical maize farm in Kedah, Malaysia using historical NASA POWER climate data. It compares possible next crops and shows missing evidence instead of inventing a recommendation.
details:
AgriShift AI is an independent student-built web application for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 Field Shift challenge. It helps users explore crop-planning questions by bringing historical NASA climate data, farmer-supplied farm details, published crop requirements, and personal priorities into one transparent workflow.

Users select a location on a map, enter soil and irrigation information, and choose a current crop. The application retrieves historical gridded rainfall and temperature from the NASA POWER Daily API, then displays monthly patterns, the observation period, data coverage, and source information. In our hypothetical Kedah, Malaysia case study, an exploratory screen compares maize followed by mung bean or sweet potato. Results show how the available information relates to broad published FAO Ecocrop ranges and identify missing evidence. Paddy, rubber, oil palm, coconut, and Robusta coffee are presented as sourced regional context; they are not given unsupported seasonal rotation scores.

The project’s creative approach is to make uncertainty part of the result. When soil information or a scientifically supported rotation model is missing, AgriShift AI explains the gap and withholds an overall ranking. This can help farmers, students, and extension officers understand what the climate record shows and what local information is still needed before making a decision.

We built the frontend with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Leaflet, and Recharts; the backend uses FastAPI, Python, Pandas, NumPy, and the NASA POWER API. We used Pytest, Vitest, GitHub Actions, and Vercel for testing, collaboration, and hosting. No special hardware is required.

The prototype does not forecast weather or yield, predict water savings, or provide validated farming recommendations. Future work requires local agronomic review of varieties, planting schedules, drainage, irrigation, and rotation rules.
